source.title: MMAligner: Safeguarding Multimodal Large Language Models through Representation Calibration
source.authors: Shenyi Zhang; Keyan Guo; Zihao Wang; Xuebin Li; Ling-Chen Zhao; Hong-Xin Hu; Chao Shen; Qian Wang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table and figure formatting is flattened, but the relevant Table 4 and Table 9 values are assignable from their layouts.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests a text-derived safety direction by adding it to multimodal safe-input representations and measuring refusal, and it tests attacks that try to suppress the direction. Its direction construction and one-layer intervention differ from the original claim’s difference-in-means direction and all-layer, all-position ablation.
record.gate_note: Table 4 directly reports refusal after adding the safety direction or control perturbations. Table 9 reports outcomes for adaptive attacks designed to suppress the direction. Table 5 reports boundary coverage and Table 3 reports intent recognition, but neither measures the intervention effects or the internal separation named by the claim versions. The MMAligner and baseline comparisons in Tables 6–8 are results for the paper’s new defense and are not included as rows for the direction itself. Layer-selection and parameter-sweep values used to choose settings are also omitted.
record.test_reason: The study adds a text-derived mean-difference direction (refused-unsafe minus safe text) at one layer to safe image+text inputs in four VLMs. It measures the induced refusal against −d̂ and orthogonal controls of equal magnitude (Table 4). This is a V1 addition test in a new multimodal setting. Table 5 also shows multimodal attack-style inputs sit below the refusal threshold along the same direction, which bears on V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that the text-learned refusal direction and boundary remain causally functional for multimodal inputs. Multimodal unsafe inputs fail because their representations shift to the non-refusal side of that boundary, not because safety capability is lost. MMAligner fine-tunes one layer to push them back across it with little utility loss.
record.recipe_differences: The safety direction is the first right-singular vector of paired refused-unsafe versus safe text representation displacements. The causal addition test intervenes at one selected layer, rather than testing the claimed mean-difference direction with ablation at every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: The target layer is selected separately for each model. LLaVA-NeXT reaches a lower refusal rate than the other models in the positive-direction addition test; the authors attribute this to weaker underlying safety alignment and a larger required perturbation.

fits_no_version.finding: A direction computed only from text-only inputs induces refusal when added to image+text inputs, at a modality-specific magnitude τ_mm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The refusal direction transfers across input modalities (text to vision-language) within a model.

fits_no_version.finding: On MMAligner-defended models, steering along −d̂ at layer l* lowers explicit refusal to 55–85%. Much of the shortfall is output collapse; coherent harmful output is 0–30%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Direction subtraction on a direction-calibrated model degrades coherence more than it restores compliance.

record.problems: The causal addition test uses 50 safe multimodal inputs per model and only one selected layer; it does not test the claimed all-layer ablation. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the Table 4 or Table 9 results. Its refusal metric uses an LLM judge, and its attack results distinguish true harmful success from output collapse.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results were omitted under the 60-row limit. Table 5 boundary-coverage measurements and Table 3 intent-recognition breakdown were not assigned rows because they do not measure the interventions or internal separation named by a tested claim version.

untested.parts: Ablation (projecting the direction out) removing refusal on harmful inputs; all-layer, all-position intervention; capability retention under the direction intervention. Only single-layer addition on safe multimodal inputs is tested.
Whether training against the direction's ablation adds robustness. Whether optimized jailbreaks on undefended models suppress the direction.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer; only text-to-image modality transfer.

missing.what: Proportion of unsafe inputs whose projection on d̂ lies inside the refusal boundary, text-only versus multimodal, per model (bears on V3: attack-style inputs reduce activation along the direction)
Dose-response of refusal on safe multimodal inputs as the magnitude along the direction increases (numbers only in figure)

record.verdict_notes: Record error: the perturbed direction d̂ is the normalized difference of means (refused-unsafe text minus safe text) at layer l* (Eq. 4–5). The first right-singular vector is only the 'safety subspace' used elsewhere, so the recipe is closer to the original than the record states. Magnitude is the median binary-searched flip threshold from 20 safe inputs. Layers: 23/29/24/30. n=50 per model, no uncertainty reported, GPT-4o-mini refusal judge. Table 9 attacks target the authors' own defended models, so the record's V3 'challenges' and 'limits_scope' labels are removed.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not ablate the direction, does not project it out at every layer and position, and does not test whether general capability remains intact after that ablation. The added-direction test is at one selected layer. Its direction is based on a principal component of paired displacements between refused unsafe and safe text inputs, not the exact difference-in-means construction in the claim.
No weight-edit conversion of an ablation or released-model abliteration is tested.
The paper tests adaptive attacks designed to suppress the direction, but does not test whether training against the direction’s ablation adds robustness.
No comparison of affine, cone, multiple-direction, or dominant-direction-plus-other-directions accounts is reported.
The intent-address check is a behavioral classification, not a test of whether harmfulness judgment and refusal are separately encoded.
The text-to-multimodal transfer experiment is not a test across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models as specified by this version.
The paper does not vary how or when refusal training is conducted to test whether that determines the existence of a removable direction.
No reasoning model is evaluated for V1.

relationships.condition: Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Llama-3.2-11B-Vision, mean-difference direction added at one layer to safe image+text inputs
relationships.reason: Adding +d̂ gave 92% and 82% refusal; equal-magnitude −d̂ and orthogonal controls gave 0% (R7, R10, R8, R9, R11, R12).

relation.reason: Its own interventional (Table 4) and projection (Table 5) results bear on whether the direction induces refusal and whether multimodal unsafe inputs lower activation along it.

tranche.reason: Applies the original method in a new setting: a text-derived mean-difference direction is added at one layer to safe image+text inputs in four VLMs, with equal-magnitude −d̂ and orthogonal controls (Table 4). It also reports projections of multimodal unsafe inputs along d̂ (Table 5). Both bear on V1 and V3. The reader's T2 fits less well because method and measure match the original's addition test.

source_check.notes: The pack's call recipe repeats the same error: it calls the safety direction the first right-singular vector, but d̂ is the normalized refused-unsafe minus safe text mean difference (Eq. 6). Fix it where it propagates. Not on the record: Table 9 steers along −d̂ on MMAligner-fine-tuned models (refusal 55–85%, true attack success 0–30%). Because those models are fine-tuned, it bears only weakly on V1 removal.

statements.correction: d̂ = Δ_text/||Δ_text||, where Δ_text = mean(refused unsafe text) − mean(safe text) at the last token (Eq. 6), taken at layer l* chosen by lowest average safe/unsafe cosine similarity (Eq. 11; Table 11). v_toxic = first right-singular vector of paired unsafe−safe displacements (Eq. 5). Table 5, share of unsafe inputs inside the refusal boundary, text→multimodal: LLaVA 31.89→0.00, LLaVA-NeXT 31.79→0.01, Qwen2.5-VL 91.56→42.59, Llama-V 88.99→51.85. Each modality uses its own boundary τ_m.
statements.problem: The pack gives no numbers for this study. Its conditions misdefine d̂: in the text, d̂ is the normalized difference in means, not the first right-singular vector. The SVD vector is v_toxic, a separate 'safety subspace'. The rest checks out: MM-SafetyBench image/typography inputs, undefended VLMs, per-model target layer, preprint, code y (github.com/shenyizg/MMAligner), and the evidence is correlational. The statement's text is cut off in the pack.

statements.correction: d̂ = normalized mean(refused unsafe text-only) − mean(safe text-only), last-token representations at layer l* (Eq. 6–7). This is a harmful-minus-harmless direction with the harmful set limited to prompts the model refused. v_toxic (first right-singular vector of paired displacements) is a separate 'safety subspace'. Drop 2608.05909 from this list, or note only the refused-only restriction.
statements.problem: Lists 2608.05909 among studies measuring something other than the harmful-minus-harmless direction, calling its direction the first right-singular vector. Wrong for the direction the results rest on: steering (Table 4), the boundary, the signed coordinate (Eq. 12) and Table 5 all use d̂, a mean difference. The SVD vector v_toxic is computed only as the 'safety subspace' (Fig. 5).
